Teacher feedback and writing quality in secondary education: a literature review
Across writing research, teacher feedback is widely treated as a mechanism for improving students’ writing quality by shaping both product (e.g., clarity, organization, accuracy) and process (e.g., planning, revision behaviors). In secondary school contexts, feedback is frequently delivered through comments on drafts, grades paired with explanatory notes, conferencing, or rubric-based guidance. Studies suggest that the effectiveness of feedback depends not only on whether students receive feedback, but also on the form, specificity, timing, and whether students actively use it to revise.

A major theme in the literature concerns feedback specificity and task relevance. Feedback that identifies particular writing issues—such as thesis clarity, paragraph cohesion, or source integration—tends to be more actionable than generalized remarks. When feedback includes concrete next steps (e.g., “move your topic sentence to the beginning of the paragraph” or “add evidence with a citation after each claim”), students are more likely to make revisions that target the writing features most associated with quality. Conversely, vague feedback can be difficult to translate into revision decisions, particularly for students who need additional support to interpret teacher language or rubric criteria.

Another recurring finding relates to the distinction between feedback that targets surface-level errors and feedback that supports deeper writing competencies. Error-focused comments (grammar, spelling, sentence-level corrections) can improve accuracy, but may yield smaller effects on higher-order qualities such as argument structure, audience awareness, and overall coherence if students do not also receive guidance on composition strategies. Many synthesis studies therefore argue for a balanced approach: teachers can address both language accuracy and writing organization, ensuring that revision efforts connect to the underlying rhetorical goals of the assignment.

Timing and opportunities for revision also matter. When teachers provide feedback early enough for students to incorporate it into subsequent drafts, feedback functions more like instruction than like evaluation. Iterative drafting—where students revise in response to comments—has been associated with improvements in writing quality compared with one-time feedback at the end of a submission. This aligns with process-oriented views of writing, in which feedback influences students’ decisions during planning and revision rather than merely highlighting shortcomings.

The literature also emphasizes feedback uptake and student agency. Effective feedback often includes explanations and supports that help students interpret comments and decide what to revise. Studies of writing motivation and self-regulation suggest that students’ beliefs about writing and their confidence in using feedback influence whether they engage deeply with teacher notes. Thus, feedback may operate through both cognitive channels (guiding revision) and motivational channels (encouraging persistence and strategy use).

Overall, research indicates that teacher feedback improves secondary students’ writing quality most reliably when it is specific, actionable, connected to the assignment’s writing goals, and paired with genuine opportunities to revise. Future work would benefit from clearer reporting of feedback types (e.g., rubric vs. narrative comments), student characteristics (e.g., writing proficiency), and implementation fidelity (e.g., whether students revise based on the feedback).

Search terms
- “teacher feedback” AND “writing quality” AND (secondary OR adolescents)
- “formative feedback” AND “writing revision”
- “feedback specificity” AND “writing”
- “error correction” AND “writing achievement” AND (secondary OR high school)
- “rubric-based feedback” AND “student revision”
- “feedback uptake” AND “writing”
- “teacher conferencing” AND “writing performance”
- “higher-order feedback” AND “argument writing”
- “process writing” AND “feedback” AND revision

Teacher feedback and students’ writing quality (secondary school): brief literature review
Teacher feedback is generally viewed as an instructional input that can improve students’ writing by guiding revision decisions. In secondary school settings, feedback is commonly provided through annotated comments, rubric-linked notes, grades with explanations, or conferencing. Research suggests that feedback effectiveness depends on whether it is actionable for students and whether it supports revisions rather than only judging final work.

One consistent theme is that more specific, concrete feedback tends to be more useful than general praise or vague criticism. Comments that name particular writing problems (e.g., thesis clarity, organization, or evidence use) and indicate how to address them can help students make targeted changes. By contrast, feedback that is too broad or ambiguous may be harder for students to interpret and convert into revisions, especially for students who are still developing writing skills.

Another theme concerns the type of feedback. Studies often distinguish between feedback focused on language accuracy (grammar, mechanics) and feedback aimed at higher-order features (structure, argument development, coherence). Error-focused feedback may improve correctness, but it may not substantially change overall quality unless students also receive guidance about the rhetorical and organizational aspects of writing. As a result, many discussions in the literature emphasize aligning feedback with the writing goals of the assignment.

Feedback timing and opportunities for revision also matter. When students can revise drafts after receiving feedback, teacher comments function more like instruction embedded in the writing process. If feedback arrives only at the end, students have limited opportunity to act on it, which can reduce its impact. Connected to this, feedback “uptake”—whether students actually use the feedback in subsequent drafts—appears important for improvements in writing quality.

Overall, the literature suggests teacher feedback can improve secondary students’ writing quality when it is specific and actionable, aligned with task goals, and accompanied by meaningful revision opportunities. Moderating factors such as students’ writing proficiency and willingness/ability to apply feedback may influence outcomes.
